'''Alice Shih-hou Huang'''<ref>{{Cite web |last=Huang |first=Alice Shih-hou |date=1966 |title=Infective and defective particles of vesicular stomatitis virus: identification, inhibition of host rna synthesis and interfering activity. |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/302209828/ |website=ProQuest}}</ref> ({{lang-zh|p=Huáng Shīhòu|w=Huang Shih-hou|c=黄诗厚}})<ref name="Huang AsianWeek">{{cite web |url=http://www.asianweek.com/2009/04/03/asian-american-heroines-alice-s-huang/ |title=Chinese American Heroines: Alice S. Huang |author=AsianWeek Staff Report |publisher=[[AsianWeek]] |date=April 3, 2009 |access-date=January 1, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090817140906/http://www.asianweek.com/2009/04/03/asian-american-heroines-alice-s-huang/ |archive-date=2009-08-17 |url-status=dead }}</ref> is a Chinese-American [[biologist]] specializing in [[microbiology]] and [[virology]]. She is currently a Senior Faculty Associate in Biology and Biological Engineering at the [[California Institute of Technology]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Alice S. Huang - Biology and Biological Engineering |url=https://www.bbe.caltech.edu/people/alice-s-huang |access-date=2026-11-10 |website=www.bbe.caltech.edu}}</ref>

She served as president of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] (AAAS) during the 2010–2011 term.<ref>{{cite web |title=AAAS Presidents |url=https://www.aaas.org/leadership/presidents |website=American Association for the Advancement of Science }}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Huang was born in the city of [[Nanchang]], Jiangxi province, China, to Quentin K. Y. Huang and Grace Betty Soong.  Her father, from [[Anhui, China]], had become an orphan at age 12 and was taken in by a missionary, eventually becoming an American educated Anglican bishop and missionary.  Her mother came from a Buddhist family with large land holdings in [[Jiangxi]] Province, and converted to Christianity.<ref name="Bhaskaran">{{cite news|last1=Bhaskaran|first1=Hillary|title=Alice Huang: Keeping Science and Life in Focus|url=http://www.typecraft.com/caltechnewsB/011999a/index.html|access-date=23 May 2015|work=Caltech News|volume=33|issue=1|date=1999|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180222043824/http://www.typecraft.com/caltechnewsB/011999a/index.html|archive-date=22 February 2018|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="Huang AsianWeek" />

She was raised Christian,<ref name="Bhaskaran"/> and emigrated to the United States in 1949.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.rockefellerfoundation.org/about-us/board-trustees/alices-huang | title=Alice S. Huang : The Rockefeller Foundation | publisher=The Rockefeller Foundation}}</ref> She attended [[St. Mary's Hall-Doane Academy]] (in Burlington, New Jersey), the [[National Cathedral School]] (in [[Washington, D.C.]]), and [[Wellesley College]] (in [[Wellesley, Massachusetts]]). Huang received her B.A., M.A., and Ph.D. (1966) degrees from [[Johns Hopkins University]]. Her doctoral dissertation was titled ''Infective and defective particles of vesicular stomatitis virus: identification, inhibition of host rna synthesis and interfering activity'' (1966).

==Career==
=== Research ===
Huang's research focused on [[defective interfering particle]]s (DIPs) which can be utilized to combat viruses. DIPs are composed of viral structural proteins and sets of DNA or RNA which are incomplete.<ref>Hannon, J. (2006). Alice Huang. Alice Huang, 1.{{full citation needed|date=July 2020}}</ref> These DIPs will interfere in replication of the virus because they are reproduced at the expense of a standard viral particle. Huang's work on DIPs has been utilized to combat cancer, HIV, and plant related diseases.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Huang |first1=Alice S. |last2=Baltimore |first2=David |title=Defective Viral Particles and Viral Disease Processes |journal=Nature |date=April 1970 |volume=226 |issue=5243 |pages=325–327 |doi=10.1038/226325a0 |pmid=5439728 |bibcode=1970Natur.226..325H |s2cid=4184206 }}</ref>

At Johns Hopkins and MIT her work for [[Robert R. Wagner]] and future husband [[David Baltimore]] was "to purify and characterize interfering viral particles".<ref name="Huang AsianWeek"/>  They studied the inhibition of cellular RNA synthesis by nonreplicating vesicular stomatitis virus, known to infect horses, cattle and swine.<ref name=pmid4317920>{{cite journal |last1=Baltimore |first1=David |last2=Huang |first2=Alice S. |last3=Stampfer |first3=Martha |title=Ribonucleic Acid Synthesis of Vesicular Stomatitis Virus, II. An RNA Polymerase in the Virion* |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |date=June 1970 |volume=66 |issue=2 |pages=572–576 |doi=10.1073/pnas.66.2.572 |pmid=4317920 |pmc=283083 |bibcode=1970PNAS...66..572B |doi-access=free }}</ref>

At the time, biologists knew the central dogma to be DNA to RNA to protein, with DNA replication as the way to replicate ones genome. Huang and Baltimore unraveled that RNA viruses were different and used RNA polymerase to replicate its RNA genome, but they discovered an enzyme, reverse transcriptase (in a mouse leukemia retrovirus), that converts RNA to DNA (involved in a process now known as reverse transcription). Baltimore later received the Nobel Prize in 1975 for his discovery.<ref name=Chung>{{cite book |last1=Chung |first1=King-Thom |chapter=Alice Shih-Hou Huang (1939-) |pages=184–190 |title=Women pioneers of medical research : biographies of 25 outstanding scientists |date=2010 |publisher=McFarland |location=Jefferson, N.C. |isbn=978-0-7864-2927-1 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=wzLkBQAAQBAJ&pg=PA184 |access-date=23 May 2015 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Bailey |first1=Martha J. |title=American Women in Science: 1950 to the Present : a Biographical Dictionary |date=1998 |publisher=ABC-CLIO |isbn=978-0-87436-921-2 }}{{page needed|date=July 2020}}</ref>

Huang and Baltimore coauthored a paper with Martha Stampfer titled "Ribonucleic acid synthesis of vesicular stomatitis virus, II. An RNA polymerase in the virion." This paper went on to show that “the virions of vesicular stomatitis virus contain an enzyme that catalyzes the incorporation of ribonucleotides into RNA”.<ref name=pmid4317920/>
  
While at Harvard Medical School, Huang continued to study how mutant strains produced by rabies-like virus interfered with further growth of the viral infection. In 1977, she was awarded the Eli Lilly Award in Microbiology and Immunology for this research.<ref name=CAFA>{{cite web|title=Alice S. Huang|url=http://physics.usc.edu/~tnchang/ahuang.htm|website=Chinese American Faculty Association, Southern California|publisher=USC University of Southern California, Department of Physics & Astronomy|access-date=23 May 2015}}</ref>  From 1971 to 1991, Huang taught at Harvard Medical School as a Microbiology and Molecular Genetics professor.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Alice S. Huang |url=https://ccst.us/people/distinguished-experts/alice-s-huang/ |access-date=2025-03-13 |website=California Council on Science & Technology (CCST) |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Administration ===

At Harvard, Huang served as coordinator of the Virology Unit at the Channing Laboratories of Infectious Diseases at [[Boston Medical Center]] for two years, and as director of the "Virus-Host Interactions in Cancer" training program (funded by the [[National Cancer Institute]]) for fifteen years.

Huang directed the Laboratories of Infectious Diseases at [[Boston Children's Hospital]] in 1979, where she studied viral diseases in pediatric patients.<ref name="Huang AsianWeek"/> At New York University, Huang participated in a project in science education and received a grant that focused on improving teachers’ preparation and ability to engage students in science exploration and discovery.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Haley-Oliphant |first1=A.E. |year=1997 |chapter=Alice Huang, Microbiologist/Molecular Geneticist, 1939-present |editor1-last=Matyas |editor1-first=M.L. |editor2-last=Haley-Oliphant |editor2-first=A.E. |title=Women Life Scientists: Past, Present, and Future: Connecting Role Models to the Classroom Curriculum |location=Bethesda, MD |publisher=American Physiological Society |pages=231–240 |oclc=932451754 }}</ref>

At New York University, Huang was appointed as dean of science; She took on the role from 1991 to 1997.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Alice S. Huang: In Research, Passion and Freedom Are Crucial to Global Progress {{!}} American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS) |url=https://www.aaas.org/news/alice-s-huang-research-passion-and-freedom-are-crucial-global-progress |access-date=2025-09-27 |website=www.aaas.org |language=en}}</ref>
 
Huang is an emeritus member of the [[board of trustees]] of the [[Keck Graduate Institute of Applied Life Sciences]] (KGI).<ref name="Huang, KGI">{{cite news |url=http://www.kgi.edu/news-and-events/feature-stories/2009/kgi-emeriti-trustee-alice-huang-elected-president-of-aaas.html |title=KGI Emeritus Trustee Alice Huang, PhD, Elected President of AAAS |publisher=[[Keck Graduate Institute of Applied Life Sciences]] |date=February 25, 2009 |place=[[Claremont, California]] |access-date=October 9, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140328220138/http://www.kgi.edu/news-and-events/feature-stories/2009/kgi-emeriti-trustee-alice-huang-elected-president-of-aaas.html |archive-date=2014-03-28 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Huang is a former trustee of the Waksman Foundation for Microbiology and a trustee of the Public Agenda. She was pointed a council member of the [[California Council on Science and Technology]] in 2004 and served for two terms.

=== Advice for Women in Science ===

In June 2015, Huang wrote an advice article<ref name="Huang 2015 Archive">{{cite web |first1=Alice |last1=Huang |date=1 June 2015 |title=Help! My adviser won't stop looking down my shirt! |work=Science Careers |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/editor-s-note |access-date=2015-06-01 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150601150626/http://sciencecareers.sciencemag.org/career_magazine/previous_issues/articles/2015_06_01/caredit.a1500140 |archive-date=June 1, 2015 }}</ref> for the Science Careers website.

A female postdoctoral scholar asked what she should do in response to her advisor looking down her shirt. Huang, who was married to [[David Baltimore|her own postdoctoral advisor]],<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2001/10/07/style/weddings-tk-baltimore-jay-konopka.html |title=WEDDINGS; TK Baltimore, Jay Konopka|date=2001-10-07|newspaper=New York Times}}</ref> replied, "I suggest you put up with it, with good humor if you can."<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Careers Staff |first1=Science |title=Better advice for 'Bothered' |journal=Science |date=4 June 2015 |doi=10.1126/science.caredit.a1500145 }}</ref> Following strong reaction on social media,<ref>{{cite web|last1=Merlan|first1=Anna|title=Science Advice Columnist: Just Let Your Adviser Stare at Your Tits|url=http://jezebel.com/science-advice-columnist-just-let-your-adviser-stare-a-1708173908|website=Jezebel|date=June 2015 |access-date=1 June 2015}}</ref> the article was removed within hours of being posted.

After the article was removed, Science Careers tweeted, "We apologize for printing it. It does not reflect our values or standards".<ref>{{cite tweet |user=ScienceCareers |author=Science Careers |number=605427695615361025 |date=1 June 2015 |title=Today's column by A. Huang has been removed.We apologize for printing it. It does not reflect our values or standards }}</ref> A fuller apology claimed the article had not "undergone proper editorial review prior to posting."<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Science Careers Staff |title=Editor's note |journal=Science |date=1 June 2015 |doi=10.1126/science.caredit.a1500140 }}</ref> In an interview,<ref>{{cite news |last1=Flaherty |first1=Colleen |title=AAAS pulls 'sexist' advice column amid outcry from readers |url=https://www.insidehighered.com/news/2015/06/02/aaas-pulls-sexist-advice-column-amid-outcry-readers |work=Inside Higher Ed |date=2 June 2015 }}</ref> Huang stood by her advice, saying, "What I try to do is give advice from experience, and to give the advice that would serve the writer well into the long-term future. I’m taking their best interests to heart rather than being in one camp or another camp or trying to push my own political agendas." She said she hoped to write a follow-up column with other people’s suggestions for dealing with the situation.

==Personal life==
Huang was married in 1968 to [[David Baltimore]]. They had one daughter.<ref>{{cite news |title=WEDDINGS; TK Baltimore, Jay Konopka |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2001/10/07/style/weddings-tk-baltimore-jay-konopka.html |work=The New York Times |date=7 October 2001 }}</ref>
